items.stem: What is the name for "transmission of a pathogen through blood or other body fluids, or touching an infected person"?
items.answer: Direct contact
items.markingKey: Direct contact: transmission of a pathogen through blood or other body fluids, or touching an infected person.

items.stem: Explain why diseases spread quickly in crowded refugee camps.
items.answer: People are close together so droplets pass easily; there may be poor sanitation and shared water supplies contaminated with faeces; poor nutrition weakens immune systems.
items.markingKey: close contact / droplets [1]; poor sanitation / water [1]; weakened defences [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why controlling mosquitoes reduces the spread of malaria.
items.answer: The mosquito is the vector carrying Plasmodium between people; fewer mosquitoes means fewer bites from infected mosquitoes.
items.markingKey: vector [1]; fewer transmissions [1] [2]

items.stem: How is cholera transmitted?
options: droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes
sexual contact, sharing needles, infected blood, mother to baby
direct contact with infected skin or contaminated surfaces (floors, towels)
items.answer: contaminated drinking water and food
items.markingKey: Cholera: caused by a bacterium (Vibrio cholerae); spread by contaminated drinking water and food.

items.stem: A health worker in Lima is trying to reduce cases of malaria. (a) State the type of pathogen that causes it. (b) Describe how it is transmitted. (c) Suggest two ways to reduce its spread.
items.answer: (a) protoctist (Plasmodium) (b) bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito (vector) (c) mosquito nets, draining standing water, insecticides
items.markingKey: (a) protoctist [1] (b) bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito (vector) [1] (c) two methods, e.g. mosquito nets, draining standing water, insecticides [2] [4]

items.stem: An outbreak of cholera occurred in a district near Istanbul. Weekly cases were: week 1: 31, week 2: 74, week 3: 120, week 4: 222. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in cases from week 1 to week 4. (b) State the type of pathogen that causes cholera and how it is transmitted.
items.answer: (a) 616% (b) bacterium (Vibrio cholerae); contaminated drinking water and food

items.stem: Which disease is caused by a protoctist and spread by a vector?
items.answer: Malaria
items.markingKey: Plasmodium is carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

items.stem: Explain why a disease such as influenza spreads faster in winter in cold countries.
items.answer: People spend more time indoors close together with less ventilation, so droplets from coughs and sneezes are breathed in more easily.
items.markingKey: indoors / close contact [1]; droplets [1] [2]

items.stem: How is tuberculosis (TB) transmitted?
options: sexual contact, sharing needles, infected blood, mother to baby
droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes
direct contact with infected skin or contaminated surfaces (floors, towels)
items.answer: droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes
items.markingKey: Tuberculosis (TB): caused by a bacterium; spread by droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes.

items.stem: Salmonella bacteria in food left at room temperature divide every 30 minutes. A piece of chicken contains 10 bacteria. Calculate how many bacteria there will be after 4 hours.
Salmonella bacteria in food left at room temperature divide every 20 minutes. A piece of chicken contains 100 bacteria. Calculate how many bacteria there will be after 5 hours.
Which is the correct definition of the term "mucus"?
options: A substance that kills or traps pathogens, such as stomach acid or mucus.
Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus up to the throat.
A physical barrier to pathogens, such as the skin or hairs in the nose.
A sticky substance made in the airways that traps pathogens and dust.
items.answer: A sticky substance made in the airways that traps pathogens and dust.
items.markingKey: Mucus: a sticky substance made in the airways that traps pathogens and dust.

items.stem: Explain how the cells lining the trachea protect the lungs from infection.
items.answer: Goblet cells make mucus that traps pathogens and dust; ciliated cells beat to sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed and acid kills the pathogens.
items.markingKey: mucus traps [1]; cilia move mucus away [1]; swallowed / removed [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why smokers get more lung infections.
items.answer: Chemicals in smoke paralyse and damage cilia, and more mucus is made, so mucus and pathogens build up in the airways.
items.markingKey: cilia damaged [1]; mucus and pathogens accumulate [1] [2]

items.stem: Which type of defence is provided by hairs in the nose?
items.answer: mechanical
items.markingKey: Hairs in the nose: mechanical defence — trap dust and pathogens in the air breathed in.

items.stem: For each defence, state whether it is mechanical, chemical or cellular, and describe how it protects the body: (i) blood clotting, (ii) lymphocytes, (iii) mucus.
items.answer: (i) mechanical: seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter (ii) cellular: produce antibodies (iii) chemical: traps pathogens in the airways
items.markingKey: (i) mechanical [1], seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter [1]; (ii) cellular [1], produce antibodies [1]; (iii) chemical [1], traps pathogens in the airways [1] [6]

items.stem: Samuel eats a sandwich that contains a small number of bacteria, and later breathes in air containing a virus in a crowded bus in Cape Town. (a) Explain how the body prevents the bacteria in the food from causing infection. (b) Explain what happens if some virus particles get past these barriers.
items.answer: (a) Hydrochloric acid in the stomach (pH 2) kills most bacteria before they reach the intestine. (b) White blood cells respond: phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens and lymphocytes produce specific antibodies.
items.markingKey: (a) acid [1]; kills bacteria [1] [2] (b) phagocytes [1]; lymphocytes / antibodies [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium.
items.answer: It moves towards the bacterium, surrounds and engulfs it into a vacuole, and digests it with enzymes.
items.markingKey: engulf [1]; digest with enzymes [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why cuts and burns increase the risk of infection.
items.answer: Damaged skin no longer forms a barrier, so pathogens can enter the body directly.

items.stem: Phagocytes were mixed with bacteria and the mean number of bacteria engulfed per phagocyte was counted: 0 min: 3, 15 min: 6, 30 min: 11, 45 min: 16, 60 min: 22. (a) Calculate the mean rate of engulfing between 0 and 60 minutes, in bacteria per phagocyte per minute. (b) Describe how phagocytes destroy the bacteria they engulf.
items.answer: (a) 0.32 (b) engulf into a vacuole and digest with enzymes
items.markingKey: (a) (22 − 3) ÷ 60 = 0.32 [2] (b) engulf [1]; digest with enzymes [1] [4]

items.stem: Phagocytes were mixed with bacteria and the mean number of bacteria engulfed per phagocyte was counted: 0 min: 3, 10 min: 7, 20 min: 11, 30 min: 17, 40 min: 20. (a) Calculate the mean rate of engulfing between 0 and 40 minutes, in bacteria per phagocyte per minute. (b) Describe how phagocytes destroy the bacteria they engulf.
items.answer: (a) 0.42 (b) engulf into a vacuole and digest with enzymes
items.markingKey: (a) (20 − 3) ÷ 40 = 0.42 [2] (b) engulf [1]; digest with enzymes [1] [4]

items.stem: For each defence, state whether it is mechanical, chemical or cellular, and describe how it protects the body: (i) lymphocytes, (ii) stomach acid, (iii) phagocytes.
items.answer: (i) cellular: produce antibodies (ii) chemical: kills pathogens in food and drink (iii) cellular: engulf and digest pathogens
items.markingKey: (i) cellular [1], produce antibodies [1]; (ii) chemical [1], kills pathogens in food and drink [1]; (iii) cellular [1], engulf and digest pathogens [1] [6]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual"?
items.answer: Passive immunity
items.markingKey: Passive immunity: short-term defence against a pathogen by antibodies acquired from another individual.

items.stem: Explain why passive immunity is only short-term.
items.answer: Antibodies received are broken down over time and no memory cells are made, so the body cannot make more antibodies.
items.markingKey: antibodies broken down [1]; no memory cells [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how vaccination programmes can protect people who have not been vaccinated.
items.answer: If most of the population is immune (herd immunity), the pathogen cannot spread easily, so unvaccinated people are less likely to meet it.
items.markingKey: most people immune [1]; pathogen spread reduced [1] [2]

items.stem: A person was vaccinated on day 0 and given a booster dose of the same vaccine on day 30. After the first dose the antibody concentration peaked at 30 arbitrary units on day 10. After the booster it peaked at 240 units on day 33. (a) Calculate how many times greater the peak was after the booster. (b) Explain the difference between the two responses.
items.answer: (a) 8 times (b) The first dose produced memory cells; on the second exposure these produced antibodies faster and in greater amounts (secondary response).
items.markingKey: (a) 240 ÷ 30 = 8 [1] (b) memory cells made after first dose [1]; faster / larger secondary response [1] [3]

items.stem: A person was vaccinated on day 0 and given a booster dose of the same vaccine on day 30. After the first dose the antibody concentration peaked at 30 arbitrary units on day 10. After the booster it peaked at 360 units on day 35. (a) Calculate how many times greater the peak was after the booster. (b) Explain the difference between the two responses.
items.answer: (a) 12 times (b) The first dose produced memory cells; on the second exposure these produced antibodies faster and in greater amounts (secondary response).
items.markingKey: (a) 360 ÷ 30 = 12 [1] (b) memory cells made after first dose [1]; faster / larger secondary response [1] [3]

items.stem: A person was vaccinated on day 0 and given a booster dose of the same vaccine on day 30. After the first dose the antibody concentration peaked at 30 arbitrary units on day 14. After the booster it peaked at 300 units on day 34. (a) Calculate how many times greater the peak was after the booster. (b) Explain the difference between the two responses. (c) Explain why this is described as active immunity.
items.answer: (a) 10 times (b) The first dose produced memory cells; on the second exposure these produced antibodies faster and in greater amounts (secondary response). (c) The person's own lymphocytes produced the antibodies and memory cells.
items.markingKey: (a) 300 ÷ 30 = 10 [1] (b) memory cells made after first dose [1]; faster / larger secondary response [1] (c) own body makes antibodies [1] [4]

items.stem: A health department in Kathmandu is running a vaccination programme against tetanus. (a) Explain why a booster dose is often given. (b) Compare active and passive immunity.
items.answer: (a) It produces a larger secondary response, increasing the number of memory cells and antibodies so protection lasts longer. (b) Active: own antibodies, memory cells, long-lasting, slower to develop. Passive: antibodies from another source, immediate, short-term, no memory cells.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) two comparisons [2]

items.stem: A health department in Cairo is running a vaccination programme against tetanus. (a) Describe how a vaccine leads to immunity. (b) Suggest why some people are given an injection of antibodies rather than a vaccine after possible exposure (for example to tetanus).
items.answer: (a) Vaccine contains weakened / dead pathogens or antigens; lymphocytes recognise antigens and produce specific antibodies; memory cells are made, giving long-term protection. (b) Antibodies act immediately, whereas a vaccine takes days to produce antibodies, which may be too slow.
items.markingKey: (a) antigens [1]; lymphocytes / antibodies [1]; memory cells [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Why does a vaccine give long-term protection?
options: It kills all pathogens in the body
It contains antibodies from another person
It causes memory cells to be made
items.answer: It causes memory cells to be made
items.markingKey: Memory cells make antibodies rapidly on re-infection.

items.stem: Explain why a second infection by the same pathogen usually produces no symptoms.
items.answer: Memory cells make large amounts of specific antibodies very quickly (secondary response), destroying the pathogen before it can reproduce enough to cause symptoms.
items.markingKey: memory cells [1]; faster, greater antibody production [1]; before symptoms [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a new influenza vaccine is needed every year.
items.answer: Influenza viruses mutate and change their antigens; antibodies and memory cells from last year no longer fit the new antigens.
items.markingKey: antigens change [1]; old antibodies not complementary [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia says: "Vaccines contain antibodies that fight the disease." Explain whether Sofia is correct.
items.answer: Vaccines contain antigens (weakened/dead pathogens) that stimulate the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Vaccines contain antigens (weakened/dead pathogens) that stimulate the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells. [2]

items.stem: A town of 80,000 people has a vaccination coverage of 60% for measles. (a) Calculate the number of people vaccinated. (b) Herd immunity needs 90% coverage. State whether the town has herd immunity and calculate how many more people (if any) need to be vaccinated.
items.answer: (a) 48,000 (b) No — 24,000 more people.

items.stem: Explain how the body develops active immunity after infection or vaccination, and why passive immunity is different.
items.answer: Antigens recognised; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies with complementary shape; antibodies mark/neutralise pathogens; memory cells remain; faster secondary response. Passive: antibodies acquired (placenta, breast milk), immediate, no memory cells, short-lived.
items.markingKey: antigen / specificity [1]; lymphocytes antibodies [1]; memory cells [1]; secondary response [1]; passive described [1]; contrast [1] [6]

(b) It produces a larger secondary response, increasing the number of memory cells and antibodies so protection lasts longer.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the safe disposal of human waste (sewage) and provision of clean water"?
items.answer: Sanitation
items.markingKey: Sanitation: the safe disposal of human waste (sewage) and provision of clean water.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "toxin"?
options: A disease caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, spread by contaminated water, causing severe diarrhoea.
A poisonous substance produced by some pathogens.
The safe disposal of human waste (sewage) and provision of clean water.
A drink of water containing salts and glucose, given to replace water and ions lost in diarrhoea.
items.answer: A poisonous substance produced by some pathogens.
items.markingKey: Toxin: a poisonous substance produced by some pathogens.

items.stem: Explain how cholera causes dehydration.
items.answer: The toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine; this lowers the water potential of gut contents, so water moves out of the blood by osmosis and is lost in watery diarrhoea.
items.markingKey: chloride ions secreted [1]; water potential lowered [1]; water leaves by osmosis [1]; diarrhoea [1] [4]

items.stem: In a district near Riyadh, there were 2615 cases of cholera in 2018. After a new water treatment plant and sewers were built, there were 728 cases in 2021. Calculate the percentage decrease in cases.

After a flood in a region near Lima, many people developed severe watery diarrhoea. Tests showed the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. (a) Explain why cholera outbreaks often follow floods. (b) Suggest two immediate actions that aid agencies should take.
items.answer: (a) Flood water mixes sewage with drinking water supplies, spreading the bacteria from faeces. (b) Provide clean drinking water (or purification tablets / boiling); provide oral rehydration solution; build temporary latrines; health education on hand washing.
items.markingKey: (a) sewage contaminates water [1]; bacteria from faeces [1] [2] (b) any two [2]

items.answer: (a) Flood water mixes sewage with drinking water supplies, spreading the bacteria from faeces. (b) Removes bacteria from faeces on hands so they are not transferred to food or water.
items.markingKey: (a) sewage contaminates water [1]; bacteria from faeces [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: A town of 25,000 people has a vaccination coverage of 85% for measles. (a) Calculate the number of people vaccinated. (b) Herd immunity needs 95% coverage. State whether the town has herd immunity and calculate how many more people (if any) need to be vaccinated.
items.answer: (a) 21,250 (b) No — 2,500 more people.

items.stem: A health department in Lima is running a vaccination programme against COVID-19. (a) Explain why a booster dose is often given. (b) Explain why it is important to vaccinate a large proportion of the population.
items.answer: (a) It produces a larger secondary response, increasing the number of memory cells and antibodies so protection lasts longer. (b) Herd immunity: the pathogen cannot spread, protecting people who cannot be vaccinated (e.g. babies, people with weak immune systems).

items.stem: A health department in Istanbul is running a vaccination programme against tetanus. (a) Explain why a booster dose is often given. (b) Explain why it is important to vaccinate a large proportion of the population. (c) Compare active and passive immunity.
items.answer: (a) It produces a larger secondary response, increasing the number of memory cells and antibodies so protection lasts longer. (b) Herd immunity: the pathogen cannot spread, protecting people who cannot be vaccinated (e.g. babies, people with weak immune systems). (c) Active: own antibodies, memory cells, long-lasting, slower to develop. Passive: antibodies from another source, immediate, short-term, no memory cells.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [2] (c) two comparisons [2]

items.stem: Explain why hand washing after using the toilet reduces the spread of disease.
items.answer: It removes pathogens from faeces on the hands, so they are not transferred to food or other people.

items.stem: A student in Lima states: "Cholera is spread by mosquitoes." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Cholera is spread by water or food contaminated with faeces containing Vibrio cholerae.
